'''''Atriplex halimus''''' (known also by its common names: '''Mediterranean saltbush''', '''sea orache''', '''shrubby orache''', '''silvery orache'''; {{IPAc-en|ˈ|ɒ|r|ə|tʃ}};<ref>{{cite encyclopedia | encyclopedia=[[Oxford English Dictionary]] third edition |title=orache |url=http://www.oed.com/view/Entry/132134 |access-date=7 December 2018| date=June 2004 |publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref> also spelled '''orach''') is a species of [[fodder]] [[shrub]] in the family [[Amaranthaceae]].

== Description ==
The plant has small gray leaves up to {{Convert|2.5|cm|abbr=off|frac=4}} long. It resembles ''[[Chenopodium berlandieri]]'' (lamb's quarters).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |title=The Complete Guide to Edible Wild Plants |publisher=[[Skyhorse Publishing]] |others=[[United States Department of the Army]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-60239-692-0 |location=New York |page=92 |language=en-US |oclc=277203364}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
The plant is widespread through the [[Mediterranean Basin]], [[North Africa|North]] and [[East Africa]] and the [[Arabian Peninsula]].<ref>{{Catalogue of Life |title=''Atriplex halimus'' L. |id=JLFD |access-date=29 December 2020}}</ref>
[[File:Bush of Atriplex halimus in Antiparos.jpg|thumb|Bush on a Mediterranean beach]]

== Ecology ==
The leaves are a dietary staple for the sand rat (''[[Psammomys obesus]]'').{{cn|date=August 2026}}

== Uses ==
The leaves are edible.<ref name=":0" /> Extracts from the leaves have shown to have significant [[hypoglycemic]] effects.<ref>[[doi:10.1007/BF00427975|Hypoglycaemic effect of the salt bush Atriplex halimus, a feeding source of Psammomys obesus]]</ref>

The species has potential use in agriculture. A study allowed sheep and goats to voluntarily feed on ''A. halimus'' and aimed to determine if the saltbush was palatable, and if so, did it provide enough nutrients to supplement the diet of these animals. In this study they determined when goats and sheep are given as much ''A. halimus'' as they like, they do obtain enough nutrients to supplement their diet – unless the animal requirements are higher during pregnancy and milk production.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Valderrabano, J., Munoz, F., Delgado |first1=I. |title=Browsing ability and utilisation by sheep and goats of Atriplex halimus L. shrubs. |journal=Small Ruminant Research |date=1996 |volume=19 |issue=2 |pages=131–136 |url=https://www.academia.edu/10164599 |access-date=13 April 2020 |location=Zaragoza, Spain|doi=10.1016/0921-4488(95)00754-7 }}</ref>

This plant is often cultivated as [[forage]] because of its [[Drought tolerance|tolerance]] for severe conditions of [[drought]], and it can grow easily in very [[Alkali soil|alkaline]] and [[Soil salinity|saline]] soils. In addition, it is useful to valorize degraded and marginal areas because it will contribute to the improvement of [[Biomass (ecology)|phytomass]] in this case.

==Use in antiquity==
According to Jewish tradition, the leaves of ''Atriplex halimus'' are known in biblical Hebrew (see: {{bibleverse|Job|30:4|31}}) as '''''maluaḥ''''' ({{Langx|he|מלוח}}),<ref>Mistranslated as "[[Malva|mallow]]s" in the [[King James Bible]] and as ''Nesseln'' ([[Urtica|nettles]]) in the [[Luther Bible]]</ref> and which are said to have been gathered and eaten by the poor people who [[Return to Zion|returned]] out of [[Babylonian captivity|Babylonian exile]] (c. 352 BCE) to build the [[Second Temple]].<ref>[[Babylonian Talmud]], ''Kiddushin'' 66a, RASHI ibid., s.v. מלוחים.</ref> Other classical Hebrew sources put the [[Mishnah|Mishnaic]] name of this edible plant as ''faʻfōʻīn'' ({{langx|he|פעפועין}}), a plant that is explained to mean ''qaqūlei'' in [[Aramaic]],<ref>[[Babylonian Talmud]] (''Erubin'' 28a, [[Rashi]] s.v. '''פעפועין'''); ibid. (''Kiddushin'' 66a, Rashi s.v. '''מלוחים'''); [[Jerusalem Talmud]] (''Peah'' 8:4, where the plant ''faʻfōʻīn'' is identified as '''קקולי''')</ref> said to be the ''al-qāqlah'' (القاقلة) in Arabic.<ref>See the Judeo-Arabic lexicon compiled by Rabbi [[Tanhum of Jerusalem|Tanḥum ben Joseph Ha-Yerushalmi]] (c. 1220–1291), entitled ''Murshid al-Kāfī'' ([[Bodleian Library]] MS. Huntington 621, frame [https://iiif.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/iiif/viewer/06abea16-07ae-4bd6-80cc-be7773bb33ae#?c=0&m=0&s=0&cv=432&r=0&xywh=-4533%2C0%2C14347%2C7138 212r]), where he explains '''פעפ"ע''' as meaning ''al-qāqlah'' (القاقلة), a plant identified as the shrubby orache (''Atriplex halimus'') in {{cite book |last=Amar|first=Z. |author-link=Zohar Amar |title=Flora of the Bible - A New Investigation Aimed at Identifying All of the Plants of the Bible in Light of Jewish Sources and Scientific Research|publisher=Rubin Mass Ltd.|date=2012 |page=166 |location=Jerusalem|language=he |oclc=783455868 }}.</ref><ref>Cf. {{cite journal |last1=Bos |first1=Gerrit |last2=Käs |first2=Fabian |author-link1=:de:Gerrit Bos |title=Arabic Pharmacognostic Literature and Its Jewish Antecedents: Marwān ibn Ǧanāḥ (Rabbi Jonah), Kitāb al-Talḫīṣ |journal=Aleph |publisher=Indiana University Press |volume=16 |issue=1 |page=186|date=2016 |doi=10.2979/aleph.16.1.145 |jstor=10.2979/aleph.16.1.145 |s2cid=171046217 |quote="''Mullāḥ'' (= saltwort). Abū Ḥanīfa said: A certain Bedouin told me that it is a variety of ''ḥamḍ'' (= sea-blite; saltwort) resembling ''al-qullām'' and it is (also called) ''qāqullā'' (= Atriplex halimus). A certain Syrian Bedouin told me: ''Al-mullāḥ'' resembles alkali plants (''ušnān'' = [[Seidlitzia rosmarinus]]). Cooked together with milk, it can be eaten; it is sweet and not salty. Its seeds can be collected like ''faṯṯ''-seeds; they can (also) be eaten baked as bread. I assume that it was called ''mullāḥ'' (lit. 'the salty') because of its color and not because of its taste." (Ibn Ǧanāḥ, ''Talḫīṣ'', fol. 50r14–v6; ed. No. 549). }}</ref>

The Greek comic poet [[Antiphanes (comic poet)|Antiphanes]] seemingly calls it halimon and refers to foraging for it in dry torrent beds.<ref>fr. 158 Kassel-Austin</ref>

The plant is mentioned again in the Middle Ages by [[Ishtori Haparchi]] in his 14th-century work ''Kaftor va-Ferach ([[Hebrew language|Hebrew]]: כפתור ופרח)'', noting that it grows in the [[Jordan Valley]] region.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Amar |first=Zohar |date=1993 |title=Estori ha-Parchi and the Identification of the Flora of Eretz Israel |journal=Proceedings of the World Congress of Jewish Studies |language=he |volume=11 |page=137 |jstor=23536280 |issn=0333-9068}}</ref>
